question: Turkish coffee is brewed in a small pot with a long handle. What is that pot called?
note: The grounds are never filtered out. They settle at the bottom of the cup, and the shapes they leave when it is turned over onto the saucer are read for fortunes. UNESCO listed the coffee in 2013 for everything around it—the making, the serving, the talking—rather than for the drink alone.

question: Lakerda, the salt-cured fish eaten with rakı, is made from which fish?
note: From torik, a large bonito. Turkish gives the bonito a new name at almost every size—vonoz, çingene palamudu, palamut, torik, altıparmak and more, up to peçuta past about sixty-five centimetres. Lakerda came into Turkish through the Greek lakérda, from a Latin name for a sea fish; the story that it comes from the Spanish la querida, the beloved, is a later one.

question: What sets lokum, sold abroad as Turkish delight, into its soft block?
note: Sugar syrup and starch are cooked together for hours until the mixture turns clear and elastic, then flavoured with rosewater, lemon or mastic and dusted so the pieces come apart. The starch version spread from a confectioner’s shop opened in İstanbul in the 1770s, still trading under the family name.

question: Simit rings are dipped in a thinned syrup before the sesame goes on. What is the syrup?
note: The dip does two jobs: it holds the seeds and it darkens the crust in the oven. The ring is two strands of dough twisted together, which is why the pattern runs around it rather than along it. It is eaten plain with tea, or split and filled with white cheese.

question: How small is a Kayseri dumpling traditionally meant to be?
note: The number is a boast about the cook’s hands rather than anything anyone counts, and it is why the parcels are pinched shut rather than folded. They are boiled, then covered with garlic yogurt and butter reddened with pepper. Other regions make them larger, and some bake them before boiling.

question: A law of 1924 pushed tea growing onto one part of the country. Which?
note: The rain and the steep slopes around Rize suited the crop, but planting at scale waited until seed arrived from Batumi in the late 1930s, and the first factory opened in 1947. Part of the reason for looking at all was coffee, which had become an expensive import once the provinces that supplied it were no longer Ottoman.

question: What makes Maraş ice cream stretch enough to be cut with a knife?
note: Salep thickens the milk and mastic resin adds the chew. Something like a thousand dried tubers go into a kilo of the flour, so collecting is restricted and exporting salep is banned outright. The stretch is also the vendor’s routine: the cone is handed over and taken back several times before it stays.

question: Hünkar beğendi sets a lamb stew on a purée of what?
note: The name means the sovereign liked it. The aubergine is burnt whole over a flame until the skin lifts, then the smoky flesh is beaten with butter, flour, milk and cheese. Aubergine runs through the names of this kitchen: karnıyarık is a split belly, imam bayıldı an imam who fainted.

question: Burn one side of a tavuk göğsü on purpose and you have which dessert?
note: Tavuk göğsü is a milk pudding thickened with chicken breast: the meat is boiled, rinsed and pulled apart until no taste of it is left and only the fibres remain, and the fibres are what give the pudding its pull. Medieval Europe did much the same in early blancmange, before gelatine took over. The scorched version is named for where the burn happens, the bottom of the cauldron, and is turned out with the burnt face upwards.

question: Pastırma is air-dried beef sealed under a paste of garlic, paprika and which seed?
note: The paste is named çemen after it, and it keeps the meat from drying faster than it cures. The word travelled further than the food: pastırma passed through Romanian and Yiddish and came out as the pastrami of New York delicatessens. Kayseri is the city most associated with the curing.

question: What has left the cone-shaped rocks of Kapadokya standing while the ground around them wore away?
choices: A hard cap over soft volcanic ash
note: Eruptions laid down a deep bed of ash that hardened into tuff, soft enough to cut with a hand tool, and a tougher layer settled over it. Where a block of the tougher rock survives it shelters the column beneath, and a cone is left behind. The same soft rock let people carve churches into the valleys and whole towns underneath them—the one at Derinkuyu goes down some eighty-five metres.

question: The white terraces at Pamukkale are built up by hot springs leaving behind what?
note: The water comes up saturated with dissolved lime and gives it back as it cools and runs downhill, so the terraces are never quite finished. The Roman city of Hierapolis stands on top, with a bathing pool into which its own columns have fallen. The Turkish name means cotton castle.

question: Hagia Sophia was finished in 537 for which emperor?
note: It went up in under six years, to a design by Anthemius of Tralles and Isidore of Miletus, who were known as mathematicians rather than as builders. The first dome came down in 558 after a run of earthquakes, and the replacement was raised higher and steeper—that is the one overhead today.

question: Roughly how old are the carved pillars at Göbekli Tepe?
note: They were raised by hunter-gatherers before pottery, metal or writing, which is what made the site so hard to fit into the sequence archaeology had settled on. The T-shaped pillars carry foxes, boars, cranes and scorpions in relief. The enclosures were deliberately filled in, which is why so much of them survived.

question: Why do the giant stone heads on Mount Nemrut sit on the ground?
choices: A later king had them removed
note: The statues stand at the tomb-sanctuary of Antiochus I, king of Commagene in the first century BC. He had himself seated among gods with both Greek and Persian names, such as Zeus-Oromasdes. The heads, about two metres tall, now stand in rows in front of the bodies they fell from.

question: How many of the Seven Wonders of the Ancient World stood in what is now Türkiye?
note: The Temple of Artemis at Ephesus and the Mausoleum at Halicarnassus, which is modern Bodrum. Little is left of either: one reassembled column marks the temple, and the tomb was quarried by crusader knights for the castle that still stands over the harbour. Its occupant, Mausolus, gave every later mausoleum its name.

question: How many main layers of settlement have archaeologists identified at Troy?
note: Heinrich Schliemann cut a trench straight down through them in the 1870s and destroyed a good deal of what he had come for. The hoard he announced as King Priam’s treasure came from a layer roughly a thousand years too early for any Trojan War. The city usually matched to Homer’s sits several levels above it.

question: The town of Safranbolu is named after a crop once grown around it. Which?
note: It was a stop on the east–west caravan route for centuries, and when the railway went elsewhere the money left with the traffic—which is why its timber-framed houses were never pulled down for better ones. UNESCO listed the town in 1994. The crop is still grown in small quantities in the villages nearby.

question: What is unusual about the water of Lake Van, the country’s largest lake?
choices: It is fresh enough to drink
It holds no fish at all
note: It is the largest soda lake in the world. Nothing flows out of it, so whatever the rivers carry in stays and concentrates, and the water is soapy enough to wash clothes in. One fish manages it, the pearl mullet, which runs up the freshwater streams each spring to spawn.

question: The Sea of Marmara takes its name from what?
choices: Marble quarried on one of its islands
note: Marmaros is Greek for marble, and the island has been quarried since antiquity—its stone went into buildings all round the ancient Mediterranean. The sea reaches the Aegean through the Dardanelles and the Black Sea through the Bosphorus, which is the whole reason İstanbul stands where it does.

category: From the Göktürks to the Ottomans
question: Before the Göktürks broke away in 552, their Rouran overlords knew them for what?
note: When Bumin asked for a Rouran princess as his bride, the Rouran khagan answered, in the Chinese records, “You are my blacksmith slave.” Bumin married a princess of the Western Wei instead, and in 552 defeated the Rouran and took the title kağan. Historians read the insult as a sign that his clan worked iron for the Rouran, not that they were slaves in a literal sense.

category: From the Göktürks to the Ottomans
question: The oldest substantial writing in a Turkic language was carved in the eighth century. Where do the stones stand?
note: Two monuments were raised in the Orhun valley in 732 and 735 for Kül Tigin and his brother Bilge Kağan, and they speak in the kağan’s own voice, warning his people against being bought off with Chinese silk and titles. The script is angular, cut for stone, and the Danish philologist Vilhelm Thomsen worked it out in 1893.

category: From the Göktürks to the Ottomans
question: Kaşgarlı Mahmud wrote the first Turkish dictionary in Baghdad in the 1070s. Who was it meant to teach Turkish to?
note: The Dîvânu Lugâti’t-Türk explains Turkish words in Arabic and was presented to the Abbasid caliph. For centuries it was known only by name, until the one surviving copy turned up in 1914 at the book bazaar in İstanbul, where Ali Emîrî bought it for 33 lira. It also holds a round map of the world as its author knew it.

category: From the Göktürks to the Ottomans
question: What happened to the Byzantine emperor captured at Malazgirt in 1071?
choices: Freed by Alp Arslan, then blinded by his own side
Held for ransom in Isfahan for ten years
Executed on the battlefield the next day
Kept at the sultan’s court for the rest of his life
note: Romanos IV Diogenes was released within about a week on terms, but Constantinople had already replaced him, and his rivals had him blinded; he died of the wounds in 1072. The battle mattered less for the men lost than for the civil war that followed, which left Anatolia open to Turkish settlement.

category: From the Göktürks to the Ottomans
question: Which city was the capital of the Selçuk state in Anatolia?
note: Rum in the old political name means Rome: the Selçuk rulers were governing land taken from the Byzantines, and said so. The Byzantines had known the city as Iconium. Rumi, who settled there and died there in 1273, carries the same word in his name—the man from Rum.

category: From the Göktürks to the Ottomans
question: How old was Mehmed II when he took Constantinople?
note: Born in 1432, he had already been put on the throne once as a boy and taken off it again. The siege of 1453 turned on a cannon cast by a Hungarian founder who had offered it to the defenders first and been told the city could not pay, and on warships dragged overland on greased timbers into the Golden Horn.

category: From the Göktürks to the Ottomans
question: Europe called Süleyman the Magnificent. What do Turks call him?
note: Kanun is the law a sultan issues himself, running alongside religious law, and his reign is when that body of rules was gathered, tidied and fixed for the next three centuries. The other titles here belong to other men: the Conqueror is Mehmed II, and the Grim is his own father, Selim I.

category: From the Göktürks to the Ottomans
question: Which building did Mimar Sinan call his masterwork?
note: He graded his own career the way a guild graded a craftsman: the Şehzade was his apprentice work, the Süleymaniye his journeyman work, and this, finished in 1575 when he was about eighty, his master’s piece. He claimed its dome had finally outdone Hagia Sophia’s, a comparison Ottoman builders had been making for a century.

category: From the Göktürks to the Ottomans
question: Where was the surviving part of Piri Reis’s 1513 world map found in 1929?
note: It came to light while the palace was being turned into a museum. About a third of the map survives, drawn on gazelle parchment, and the notes in its margins say it was compiled from older charts, one of them belonging to Columbus. What it shows of the Atlantic coast is why it is famous.

category: From the Göktürks to the Ottomans
question: The first press printing in Turkish in the Ottoman Empire opened in the 1720s. What did its licence refuse to cover?
note: İbrahim Müteferrika’s licence from Ahmed III covered dictionaries, history, geography and science, and the first volume off the press in 1729 was an Arabic-Turkish dictionary. Presses working in Hebrew, Armenian and Greek had been running in the city for two centuries by then; what was new was Turkish in movable type.

question: What did Mahmud II destroy in 1826, in the episode called Vaka-i Hayriye?
note: The name of the episode means the auspicious event, which is the government’s word for it rather than the corps’. It had begun as a standing infantry raised from Christian boys taken as a levy—yeni çeri, the new troop, is the phrase English borrowed as janissary—and had become a political body able to unseat sultans. An overturned soup cauldron had long been its own signal that it was in revolt, and when it rose against a new European-style army its barracks were shelled.

question: The Tanzimat reforms opened in 1839 with an edict promising what?
choices: Equality before the law for every religion
note: It was read out in the rose garden of Topkapı, which is what the edict is named after, and it also promised security of life and property and an orderly way of taking tax. How much of it reached daily life is argued over; that the state announced it at all was new. The era it opened ran to 1876.

question: Anzac Day, kept each April in Australia and New Zealand, remembers landings on which peninsula?
note: The campaign of 1915 was meant to force the straits and reach İstanbul quickly; it became a stalemate and ran eight months. In Turkish it is remembered by the name of the town at the narrows, Çanakkale, and it is where Mustafa Kemal made his name as a commander.

question: The Grand National Assembly first met in Ankara on 23 April 1920. What else does that date mark now?
note: The assembly gathered while the capital was under foreign occupation and declared itself the only lawful authority in the country. The day was given over to children in 1929, and schools still hand their seats to them for it—it is usually described as the first national holiday anywhere dedicated to children.

question: Which treaty replaced the Treaty of Sèvres and settled the new republic’s borders?
note: It was signed in July 1923 after eight months of talks led on the Turkish side by İsmet, who later took his surname from the battles he had fought at İnönü. It cancelled the partition Sèvres had set out, and it provided for an exchange of populations with Greece that moved well over a million people.

question: Ankara’s old name, Angora, lives on in the names of which animals?
choices: A goat, a cat and a rabbit
A horse, a dog and a hen
A sheep, a camel and a hawk
A cow, a duck and a mule
note: The Angora goat gives mohair, and the long-haired cat and rabbit carry the same name; Europeans called the city Angora until 1930. It became the capital on 13 October 1923, a fortnight before the republic was proclaimed, when it was an inland town of a few tens of thousands. It was chosen because it was central, defensible, and not İstanbul, which had spent the previous years under occupation.

question: The sultanate ended in 1922. What did the assembly abolish in March 1924?
note: The last sultan had left in 1922, and a cousin, Abdülmecid II, had stayed on holding the religious office alone. When that went too he was put on a train out of the country the next day. Ottoman sultans had claimed the title since the sixteenth century.

question: Turkish has been written in a Latin alphabet since 1928. Which of these letters does it not use?
note: The alphabet has 29 letters: q, w and x were left out, and ç, ğ, ı, ö, ş and ü were added for Turkish sounds. J stayed, mostly for borrowed words such as jandarma. The law passed on 1 November 1928 and left only months to change over, and Atatürk toured the country with a blackboard, teaching the letters himself.

question: Turkish women won the vote in national elections in 1934. Which of these countries gave it to women later?
note: French women got the national vote in 1944 and Italian women in 1946; Germany had given it in 1918, the United States in 1920, and Britain in 1918 to older women and in 1928 on equal terms. In Türkiye the municipal vote had come in 1930. At the 1935 election, the first in which women could vote, eighteen women were elected to the assembly.

question: The Surname Law of 1934 made family names compulsory. How did Mustafa Kemal come by his?
choices: The assembly voted it to him
note: A law of its own granted it that November and barred anyone else from taking it. Before the reform most people were known by a given name with a father’s name, a trade or a birthplace attached, and registrars spent months helping households invent new ones.

question: Which English word was borrowed from the Turkish köşk?
note: A köşk was a garden pavilion, open along its sides; several stand in the grounds of Topkapı. French took the word as kiosque, and in the nineteenth century it settled onto the little structures put up in streets and parks to sell newspapers. English has other Turkish loans: yogurt, horde from ordu, and bosh from boş, meaning empty.

question: How does the knot used in Anatolian carpets differ from the Persian one?
choices: It is tied round a single warp
It is symmetrical, tied round two warps
It is glued rather than tied
It uses two colours in each knot
note: The symmetrical knot is also called the Gördes knot, after a weaving town, and it gives a sturdier pile; the asymmetrical Persian knot can be packed tighter, which suits fine detail. Turn a rug over and the knots show, which is the first thing anyone buying one is taught to do.

question: İznik pottery is known for a red that stands slightly proud of the surface. What was the pigment?
note: The colour, called bole, appears around the 1550s and is thick enough to feel with a fingertip. Before it, İznik worked mostly in blue and white in imitation of Chinese porcelain. The body underneath is not ordinary clay but a paste of ground quartz, which is what makes the white so bright beneath the glaze.

question: In ebru, where is the pattern made before it reaches the paper?
note: The water is thickened with tragacanth so the colours float instead of sinking; they are flicked on with a horsehair brush and drawn about with a fine point. Laying paper on top lifts the pattern and destroys it in the same movement, so no two sheets can match. UNESCO listed the craft in 2014.

question: What are the figures in Karagöz shadow theatre made of?
note: Camel or ox hide is scraped thin enough for the colour to come through when the figure is held against the lit screen. The pair at the centre are opposites—one blunt and unschooled, the other full of book learning—and the comedy is in one misunderstanding the other. UNESCO listed the form in 2009.

question: In the Mevlevi sema, how does the turner hold the hands?
choices: Right palm up, left palm down
note: The raised palm is said to take what is given and the lowered one to pass it on, keeping nothing. The tall felt hat stands for the gravestone of the ego and the black cloak for the grave itself, which is why the cloak is dropped before the turning starts.

question: What are the wrestlers at the Kırkpınar festival covered in?
note: The oil makes every hold slide, so bouts can run long and are won by lifting an opponent or turning him onto his back. The leather trousers, kıspet, are the only thing left to grip. Ottoman records put annual contests outside Edirne back in the fourteenth century, and the winner takes the title of chief wrestler.

question: In the best-known Nasreddin Hoca story, why is he hunting outside for a ring he lost indoors?
choices: Because a neighbour told him to
Because he had already searched inside
Because his wife had locked him out
note: The joke is old and travels well: versions are told across the Balkans, the Middle East and Central Asia, sometimes about other wise fools entirely. He is usually placed in the thirteenth century, and his tomb stands at Akşehir.

question: Which Turkish film won the Palme d’Or at Cannes in 2014?
choices: Bir Zamanlar Anadolu’da (Once Upon a Time in Anatolia)
note: Nuri Bilge Ceylan’s three-hour film is set in a small hotel cut into the rock of Kapadokya and turns almost entirely on arguments between the people inside it. It was the first Turkish winner since Yol in 1982, which Yılmaz Güney wrote in prison and had filmed to his instructions by Şerif Gören.

question: Which writer won the country’s first Nobel Prize, in 2006?
note: The citation spoke of a quest for the melancholy soul of his native city. He later opened the Museum of Innocence in İstanbul, which shows the objects described in his novel of the same name. Aziz Sancar became the second Turkish Nobel laureate, in chemistry, in 2015.
